title: Performance Tracker API
description: Application metrics for the Performance Tracker (api and cron jobs). EC2 host metrics live in the Node Exporter Full dashboard.

panels.title: Targets up
panels.description: How many of the 3 jobs (api, cron, node) Prometheus can scrape.

panels.title: Queue: dead letter
panels.description: Events that exhausted their retries. max() because the gauge is exposed by both the api and cron jobs, which query the same Postgres; sum() would double it.

panels.title: Queue: failed
panels.description: Awaiting retry. max() because the gauge is exposed by both the api and cron jobs, which query the same Postgres; sum() would double it.

panels.title: Queue: pending
panels.description: Received, not processed yet. max() because the gauge is exposed by both the api and cron jobs, which query the same Postgres; sum() would double it.

panels.title: Requests/s by route
panels.description: Rate per mounted route; concrete URLs never become labels. A request that matched no handler is route="unmatched", and CORS preflight, which the cors middleware answers before routing, is route="cors-preflight". Preflight used to land in unmatched and drown it: 697/s against 0.0/s of real 404s.

panels.title: Latency p50 / p95 / p99
panels.description: Percentiles over the histogram buckets, every route that does work. CORS preflight is excluded: it is answered in microseconds and there is more of it than there is real traffic, so including it understated these. Measured at the time of the change, it pulled p95 from 7.4s down to 4.5s and p50 from 28ms to 8ms, which reads as an API far faster than it is.

panels.title: Latency p99 by route (top 5)
panels.description: The panel above says something is slow; this one says what. Read it with the one beside it, never alone: a route with a handful of requests can post a dramatic p99 off a single slow call and outrank a route that is actually shaping the aggregate. Latency here, weight there.

panels.title: Requests slower than 0.5s, by route (top 5)
panels.description: Who actually draws the aggregate p99. The p99 line is the slowest 1% of requests, so the route supplying most of them sets it, however healthy everything else is. Measured over one 6h window: 98.6% of requests finished under 0.5s, and of the 1,588 that did not, /api/time-tracker/init supplied 68.5%, which was the whole of the p99 people were asking about. Its median equals the mean WebWork call it waits on, 0.54s against 0.539s, so the number was never about the database or the pool. Note the bucket label is le="0.5": these carry a decimal, and le="0.50" matches nothing and paints an empty panel that reads as good news.

panels.title: 5xx error rate
panels.description: Share of requests answered with 5xx. CORS preflight is out of the denominator: it never fails, so counting it dilutes the ratio by however much protocol overhead happens to be flowing. Phase 6 alert fires above 0.05.

panels.title: Requests/s by status
panels.description: Useful for spotting 4xx climbing before it turns into an incident.

panels.title: Users refused
panels.description: Distinct signed-in users that got a 4xx or 5xx in this window. The number is the shape of the problem: two is somebody's bad afternoon, and 186 was the render loop of 2026-08-11. Unauthenticated requests are excluded here, so this can read one lower than the bar gauge below, which does show them.

targets.expr: count(count by (userId) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" | userId != "" [$__range])))

panels.title: Tenants refused
panels.description: Distinct tenants behind those users. One tenant with many users is a client whose whole office is affected; many tenants is ours.

targets.expr: count(count by (tenantId) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" | tenantId != "" [$__range])))

panels.title: Refusals
panels.description: Every 4xx and 5xx the API answered in this window, including the 429s the rate limiter produced.

panels.title: Users refused most (top 10)
panels.description: One bar per user id. The empty bucket is renamed rather than hidden: requests with no user are unauthenticated traffic, which is worth seeing next to the rest instead of silently dropped. Concentration is the signal here, not the total. On 2026-08-11 four people out of 139 supplied 55% of a million refusals, and every one of them was a browser tab in a render loop rather than a person doing anything.

targets.expr: label_replace(topk(10, sum by (userId) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" [$__range]))), "userId", "(not signed in)", "userId", "^$")

panels.title: Tenants refused most (top 10)
panels.description: The same window grouped by tenant. Read it against the panel beside it: one tenant made of one user is a single stuck client, and one tenant made of many is something that reached the whole office.

targets.expr: label_replace(topk(10, sum by (tenantId) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" [$__range]))), "tenantId", "(no tenant)", "tenantId", "^$")

panels.title: Paths refused most (top 10)
panels.description: path is the normalised url, ids collapsed to :id and the query string dropped. It is recorded only when no handler matched, which is the case for everything the rate limiter refuses, so this is the panel that separates /api/time-tracker/init from /api/time-tracker/start - one label upstairs, two very different problems. A request that did reach a handler has no path and is named by the bucket instead.

targets.expr: label_replace(topk(10, sum by (path) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" [$__range]))), "path", "(a handler matched, see route)", "path", "^$")

panels.title: Refusals by status over time
panels.description: A range query rather than a top-N: statusCode is a closed set, so it cannot blow up the way a user or path grouping would. Each point is a count inside one interval bucket, not a rate, which is how the logs board draws the same shape. 429 climbing on its own is the rate limiter doing its job against a client that will not stop; 401 and 403 climbing together is usually a session or company-scope problem.

targets.expr: sum by (statusCode) (count_over_time({job="server"} | json | msg=~"request rejected|request failed" [$__interval]))

panels.title: Event loop lag p99
panels.description: Event loop delay per process. Phase 6 alert fires above 0.2.

panels.title: Heap used
panels.description: V8 heap in use, per process.

panels.title: Restarts per hour
panels.description: process_start_time_seconds changes whenever the process restarts. Deploys count too (pm2 reload). Phase 6 alert fires above 3/h.

panels.title: Waiting for a connection
panels.description: Queries queued because every connection is checked out. Anything sustained above zero means the pool is the bottleneck, not the database and not CPU. On 2026-07-30 this shape produced 503s from the API Gateway while the app itself never returned a 5xx.

panels.title: In use and available
panels.description: Checked out against idle. Available at zero with in use at the ceiling is the saturated state; read it together with the waiting panel.

panels.title: Saturation against the configured ceiling
panels.description: in use over db_pool_max, so the limit is not hardcoded here. The ceiling is per process, so two api workers at 100% is twice the connections of one.

panels.title: Queues over time
panels.description: max() deduplicates: the gauges arrive from both the api and cron jobs with the same value.

panels.title: Webhook processing p95
panels.description: Time spent dispatching an event to its handler, by type.

panels.title: Webhooks received/s by type
panels.description: Emitted by the api job — webhooks come in through the API.

panels.title: Events processed/s by status
panels.description: Emitted by the cron job. status=failed climbing precedes dead letter growth.

panels.title: Errors and warnings
panels.description: Error and warning lines from the API, read from the level field. filename tells the two clustered instances apart (server-out-8 vs server-out-9). Lines that fail to parse are kept: those are the crashes that never reach the logger, and dropping them would hide exactly the worst failures.
